facts.statement: Edestus was an extinct genus of eugeneodontid holocephalian fish found in the Late Carboniferous of the United Kingdom, Russia, and the United States.
facts.quote: Edestus is an extinct genus of eugeneodontid holocephalian fish known from the Late Carboniferous (Pennsylvanian) of the United Kingdom, Russia, and the United States.

facts.statement: The name Edestus is Greek for 'to devour', referring to the unusual quality and large size of its teeth.
facts.quote: Edestus is a Greek name derived from the word edeste (to devour), in reference to the aberrant quality and size of the species' teeth.

facts.statement: The largest species, E. heinrichi, was conservatively estimated to exceed 6.7 meters (22 feet) in length, potentially making it the largest marine predator known up to that point in history.
facts.quote: The largest species, E. heinrichi, has been conservatively estimated to reach greater than 6.7 m (22 ft) in length, around the size of the largest known great white shark, possibly making it the largest marine predator known to have ever existed up to that point.

facts.statement: Edestus had a single row of teeth in the midline of each jaw, earning it the nickname 'scissor tooth shark'.
facts.quote: In Edestus' case, only a single row of teeth occurred in the midline of each jaw, leading Edestus to sometimes be described as the "scissor tooth shark".

facts.statement: Edestus was first described by Joseph Leidy in 1856.
facts.quote: Edestus was first described by Joseph Leidy in 1856.

facts.statement: The type species Edestus vorax has a holotype specimen (ANSP 9899) that is very fragmentary, with its origin reported as Muskogee County, Oklahoma, though this location is disputed.
facts.quote: The type species is Edestus vorax, the holotype specimen (ANSP 9899) is very fragmentary and of uncertain stratigraphic and geographic provenance, reported to be from Muskogee County, Oklahoma, though this has been questioned.

facts.statement: Edestus minor was described in 1866 by John Strong Newberry based on a single crown found in Posey County, Indiana.
facts.quote: Edestus minor was described in 1866 by John Strong Newberry based on AMNH FF477, a single crown that lacks most of the root from Posey County, Indiana.

facts.statement: Edestus heinrichi was described in 1870 by Newberry and Amos Henry Worthen from a specimen found in Illinois that is now lost.
facts.quote: Edestus heinrichi was described in 1870 by Newberry and Amos Henry Worthen from a now-lost specimen found in Illinois.

facts.statement: Edestus karpinskii was described in 1908 by A.B. Missuna from remains found near Kolomna, approximately 100 km southeast of Moscow.
facts.quote: Edestus karpinskii was described by A.B. Missuna in 1908 from remains found near Kolomna around 100 km southeast of Moscow.

facts.statement: Edestus tooth whorls consisted of numerous serrated teeth with long V-shaped roots stacked on top of each other like roof tiles.
facts.quote: The whorls of Edestus are composed of numerous serrated teeth that have long v-shaped roots that are stacked on top of each other akin to roof tiling.

facts.statement: Edestus teeth grew at the back of the whorl, migrated forward through it, and were ejected from the front.
facts.quote: Teeth grew in the back end (posterior) of the whorl, and gradually migrated forward through the whorl, before being ejected at the front end (anterior).

facts.statement: The upper and lower tooth whorls of Edestus differed in shape, with the lower whorl being more curved.
facts.quote: The upper and lower whorls are distinct in their morphology, with the lower whorl having a greater degree of curvature.

facts.statement: A preserved juvenile specimen (FMNH PF2204) had a cranium about 25 cm long with associated upper and lower whorls measuring 10.4 cm and 8 cm respectively.
facts.quote: The cranium of FMNH PF2204 is around 25 cm in length, and the associated upper and lower whorls have lengths of 10.4 and 8 cm, respectively.

facts.statement: The largest known individuals of E. heinrichi possessed an upper whorl 32 cm long and a lower whorl 43 cm long.
facts.quote: The largest known individuals of E. heinrichi are an upper whorl 32 cm in length and a lower whorl 43 cm in length.

facts.statement: Although 13 species of Edestus have been named, a 2019 analysis validated only four species spanning a six-million-year interval from 313 to 307 million years ago.
facts.quote: 13 species of Edestus have been named, but in a 2019 morphometric analysis only 4 were considered valid, which span a six million year interval in the Late Carboniferous (313-307 million years ago).

facts.statement: Edestus species are divided into two groups based on whether their tooth crowns are asymmetrical and slanting forward or symmetrical.
facts.quote: Species of Edestus are divided into two groups, those which have asymmetrical crowns that slant forwards, and those with symmetrical ones.

facts.statement: The earliest Edestus species appear in the late Bashkirian of the UK, with later appearances in Russia and the US during the Moscovian, coinciding with a rise in sea level.
facts.quote: The earliest known species are from the late Bashkirian of the United Kingdom, with the first appearances in Russia and the United States during the Moscovian, corresponding to a rise in sea level.

facts.statement: E. triserratus is distinguished by obtuse triangular crowns narrowing to a bullet-shaped apex, fine denticles, and a massive straight upper whorl base with a slender, tightly curved lower whorl.
facts.quote: E. triserratus Newton, 1904 (syn Edestus minusculus Hay, 1909, Edestodus kolomnensis (Lebedev, 2001)) Late Bashkirian to Moscovian, United States, United Kingdom and Russia distinguished by having obtuse triangular crowns that narrow to a "bullet shaped" apex, the denticles are fine and the root is proportionally longer than E. minor upper whorl has a massive straight base, while the lower whorl is slender and more tightly curved

facts.statement: The species E. heinrichi has several synonyms including E. protopirata, Protopirata centrodon, E. karpinskyi, E. crenulatus, and E. serratus.
facts.quote: E. heinrichi Newberry and Worthen, 1870 (syn E. protopirata Trautschold, 1879, Protopirata centrodon Trautschold, 1888, E. karpinskyi Missuna, 1908, E. crenulatus Hay, 1909, E. serratus Hay, 1909)

facts.statement: E. heinrichi is distinguished by crowns with an acute triangular shape, a longer posterior edge, coarse denticles, and roots that are straight in the upper whorl but curved in the lower whorl.
facts.quote: distinguished by having crowns with an acute triangular shape, with a slightly longer posterior than anterior edge, coarse denticles, and long and straight roots in the upper whorl, slightly curved in the lower whorl

facts.statement: E. vorax, described by Leidy in 1856, has crowns with an acute triangular shape, a longer posterior edge, very coarse denticles, and stout roots extending deep beneath the crown.
facts.quote: E. vorax Leidy, 1856 (syn E. giganteus Newberry, 1889) Moscovian of the United States distinguished by crowns with acute triangular shape, a slightly longer posterior edge, very coarse denticles, stout roots that extend deep beneath the tooth crown, and intermediate apex angle

facts.statement: E. newtoni, described by Arthur Smith Woodward in 1916 from the Millstone Grit of Yorkshire, has a much greater whorl curvature than other species and has sometimes been placed in the separate genus Lestrodus.
facts.quote: Edestus newtoni, described by Arthur Smith Woodward in 1916 from the "Millstone Grit" of Yorkshire, United Kingdom, has a much greater curvature of the whorl than other species of Edestus, and has sometimes been placed in its own genus Lestrodus.

facts.statement: A specimen described by Oliver Hay in 1912 as E. mirus preserved two whorls attached to jaw cartilage, definitively showing the whorls were situated in the mouth.
facts.quote: The specimen described by Oliver Hay in 1912 as Edestus mirus preserved two whorls still attached to fragments of jaw cartilage, and definitively showed that the whorls were situated in the mouth.

facts.statement: A 2018 redescription by Tapanila and colleagues found that less curved tooth whorls in some Edestus species functioned as grasping and slicing tools for soft-bodied prey like cephalopods.
facts.quote: Their detailed 2018 redescription of the cranial material of Edestus, Tapanila and colleagues found that the less curved tooth whorls of some Edestus species functioned as effective grasping and slicing tools for soft bodied prey such as cephalopods.

facts.statement: Most Edestus remains are found in marine shales overlying coal swamp deposits due to marine transgression, though the genus is also known from estuarine habitats.
facts.quote: Most remains of Edestus are found in marine shales that overlie coal swamp deposits as a result of marine transgression events, but the genus is known from estuarine habitats as well.

facts.statement: Edestus lived during the Upper Carboniferous, from the Bashkiriense to the Moscoviense stages.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Carbonífero Superior (Bashkiriense a Moscoviense)

facts.statement: Edestus is classified in the kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Chondrichthyes, order Eugeneodontiformes, and family Edestidae.
facts.quote: regnum: Animalia phylum: Chordata classis: Chondrichthyes subclassis: Holocephali/Selachimorpha? ordo: Eugeneodontiformes familia: Edestidae

facts.quote: genus_authority: Leidy, 1856

facts.statement: Edestus is an extinct genus of cartilaginous fish of the order Eugeneodontiformes, known from Upper Carboniferous (Pennsylvanian) fossils in the United Kingdom, Russia, and the United States.
facts.quote: Edestus es un género extinto de peces cartilaginosos del orden Eugeneodontiformes, conocido a partir de restos fósiles del Carbonífero Superior (Pensilvaniense) del Reino Unido, Rusia y los Estados Unidos.

facts.statement: The name Edestus is derived from the Greek word edeste (devour), referring to the strange qualities and size of the teeth of this genus.
facts.quote: Edestus es un nombre derivada de la palabra griega edeste (devorar), en referencia a las extrañas cualidades y el tamaño de los dientes de este género.

facts.statement: The largest species, E. heinrichi, has been conservatively estimated to be over 6.7 meters in length, a size close to that of the largest great white shark.
facts.quote: La especie más grande, E. heinrichi, ha sido estimado en forma conservadora en un tamaño mayor a los 6.7 metros de longitud, un tamaño cercano al del mayor gran tiburón blanco.

facts.statement: In Edestus, only a row of teeth appeared in the middle zone of each jaw, giving it an appearance described as a "shark with scissors teeth".
facts.quote: En el caso de Edestus, solo aparecía una fila de dientes en la zona media de cada mandíbula, dándole a Edestus una apariencia que ha sido descrita como la de un "tiburón con dientes de tijera".

facts.statement: In 1855, Edward Hitchcock presented an Edestus specimen at a meeting of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in Providence; the specimen, a toothed frond, was originally found in Parke County, Indiana.
facts.quote: En 1855 Edward Hitchcock presentó un espécimen de Edestus en un encuentro de la Asociación Estadounidense para el Avance de la Ciencia en Providence (Rhode Island); el ejemplar, una fronda con dientes había sido hallado originalmente en el condado de Parke en Indiana.

facts.statement: The specimen was lent to British anatomist Richard Owen in 1861, who referred it to Edestus and suggested it was a fin spine.
facts.quote: El espécimen fue dado en préstamo al famado anatomista británico Richard Owen en 1861, quien refirió dicho espécimen a Edestus y sugirió que era una espina de una aleta.

facts.statement: E. minor was described in 1866 by John Strong Newberry based on specimen AMNH FF477, a single tooth crown lacking most of the root, found in Posey County, Indiana.
facts.quote: Edestus minor fue descrito en 1866 por John Strong Newberry con base en el espécimen AMNH FF477, una única corona dental que carece de la mayor parte de la raíz y fue hallado en el condado de Posey, Indiana.

facts.statement: E. heinrichi was discovered in 1870 by Newberry and Amos Henry Worthen from a specimen now lost, found in Illinois.
facts.quote: Edestus heinrichi fue descubierto en 1870 por Newberry y Amos Henry Worthen a partir de un espécimen ahora perdido hallado en Illinois.

facts.statement: E. triserratus was described in 1904 by Edwin Tulley Newton from specimen GSM 31410, found in coal mines in Staffordshire, England, consisting of a partial tooth lacking the crown apex.
facts.quote: Edestus triserratus fue descrito en 1904 por Edwin Tulley Newton, a partir del espécimen GSM 31410, el cual fue hallado en los yacimientos de carbón de Staffordshire, en Inglaterra, consistiendo en un diente parcial que carece del ápice de la corona.

facts.statement: Oliver Perry Hay was the first to describe an associated pair of upper and lower fronds (USNM V7255) found in a coal mine near Lehigh, Iowa, which he assigned to the new species E. mirus, now considered a synonym of E. minor.
facts.quote: Oliver Perry Hay en 1912 fue el primero en describir una pareja asociada de frondas superior e inferior (USNM V7255), hallada en una mina de carbón cerca de Lehigh (Iowa), la cual él asignó a la nueva especie Edestus mirus, que se considera como un sinónimo de Edestus minor.

facts.statement: E. karpinskii was described by A.B. Missuna in 1908 from remains found near Kolomna, about 100 kilometers southeast of Moscow.
facts.quote: Edestus karpinskii fue descrito por A.B. Missuna en 1908 a partir de restos encontrados cerca de Kolomna, alrededor de 100 kilómetros al sureste de Moscú.

facts.statement: E. minusculus was described by Hay in 1912 from a specimen originally described by Alexander Karpinsky as E. cf. minor, found in the Myachkova quarry near Moscow.
facts.quote: Edestus minusculus fue descrito por Hay en 1912 de un espécimen descrito originalmente por Alexander Karpinsky como Edestus cf. minor el cual fue hallado en la cantera de Myachkova, cerca de Moscú.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the tooth whorls were attached to the dorsal fin, as proposed by Edwin Newton, or to the pectoral fins, as believed by Edward Drinker Cope.
facts.quote: Researchers such as Edwin Newton proposed it was likely attached to the dorsal fin specifically, while other such as Edward Drinker Cope believed they were paired structures attached to the pectoral fins.

facts.statement: Following detailed skull descriptions in 2004, researchers proposed two alternative feeding strategies: either an active predator ramming fish and using whorls like scissors, or a specialist jellyfish feeder.
facts.quote: Following the first detailed descriptions of the genus' skull in 2004, researchers Rainer Zangerl and Clifford Jeremiah proposed two alternative feeding strategies: either it was an active predator which killed fish by ramming them with its mouth open and then using its whorls like scissors to cut them apart, or it was a specialist jellyfish feeder.

facts.statement: The fronds of Edestus consisted of numerous serrated teeth with long V-shaped roots stacked like roof tiles.
facts.quote: Las frondas de Edestus se componen de numerosos dientes aserrados que tienen largas raíces en forma de V que se apilan uno sobre otro de forma similar a las piezas de un tejado.

facts.statement: More than a dozen teeth were present on each frond at any given time.
facts.quote: Más de una docena de dientes estaban presentes en cada fronda en un momento dado.

facts.statement: The animal may have had over 40 teeth on each frond throughout its life.
facts.quote: El animal puede haber tenido más de 40 dientes en cada fronda a lo largo de su vida.

facts.statement: The largest individuals of E. heinrichi had an upper frond 32 centimeters long and a lower frond 43 centimeters long.
facts.quote: Los individuos más grandes de E. heinrichi tienen una fronda superior de 32 centímetros de largo y la inferior de 43 centímetros de longitud.

facts.statement: Based on a body-to-head length ratio of 5:1, the largest individuals of E. heinrichi could reach total lengths of 6.7 meters.
facts.quote: Con base en una proporción de longitud de cuerpo a cabeza de 5:1, se sugiere que los mayores individuos de E. heinrichi podían alcanzar longitudes totales de 6.7 metros.

facts.statement: Eugeneodontes with preserved postcrania include caseodontoids from the Upper Carboniferous to Triassic of the genera Caseodus, Fadenia, and Romerodus.
facts.quote: Los eugeneodontes con postcráneos preservados incluyen caseodontoideos del Carbonífero Superior al Triásico, de los géneros Caseodus, Fadenia y Romerodus.

facts.statement: This general body plan is shared with active open-ocean predatory fish such as tuna, swordfish, and lamnid sharks.
facts.quote: Este plan corporal general es compartido con peces depredadores activos de mar abierto tales como el atún, el pez espada y los tiburones lámnidos.

facts.statement: Eugeneodontes lacked pelvic and anal fins, and judging by Romerodus, they likely had broad keels along the body sides extending to the tail fin.
facts.quote: Los eugeneodontes además carecían de aletas pélvicas y anales, y al juzgar por Romerodus, ellos habrían tenido amplias quillas a lo largo de los costados del cuerpo hasta llegar a la aleta caudal.

facts.statement: Fadenia likely had five well-exposed gill slits, possibly with a sixth vestigial slit.
facts.quote: Fadenia habría tenido cinco hendiduras bien expuestas para las branquias, posiblemente con una sexta hendidura vestigial.

facts.statement: There is no evidence that they possessed the specialized gill basket and fleshy operculum found in modern chimaeriforms.
facts.quote: No hay evidencia de que tuvieran la cesta branquial especializada y el opérculo carnoso presente en los actuales quimeriformes.

facts.statement: The chondrocranium was encapsulated in a dorsal plate resembling a shield.
facts.quote: El condrocráneo estaba encapsulado en una placa dorsal a modo de escudo.

facts.statement: Tapanila and colleagues (2018) determined that the dental fronds functioned as effective tools for grasping and cutting soft-bodied prey.
facts.quote: Tapanila y colaboradores (2018) determinaron que las frondas dentales funcionaban como herramientas efectivas para asir y cortar presas de cuerpo blando.

facts.statement: The jaws of Edestus operated in a two-gear system involving the double articulation of the quadrate bone, allowing forward and backward jaw movements similar to streptostyly in modern lizards, with an output force of 1,907 newtons.
facts.quote: Las mandíbulas de Edestus operaban en un sistema de dos engranajes, involucrando la doble articulación del hueso cuadrado que permitía movimientos hacia adelante y hacia atrás de la mandíbula, de modo similar a la estreptostilia vista en los actuales reptiles escamosos, con una fuerza de salida de 1,907 newtons.

facts.statement: These localities were situated in paleo-equatorial tropical latitudes.
facts.quote: Estas localidades se situaban en latitudes tropicales paleoecuatoriales.

facts.statement: Many Edestus remains have been found in marine shales overlying swamp coal deposits as a result of marine transgression events.
facts.quote: Muchos de los restos de Edestus se han encontrado en esquistos marinos que se superponen a depósitos de carbón de pantanos como resultado de eventos de transgresiones marinas.

facts.statement: E. triserratus lived from the upper Bashkirian to Moscovian in the US, UK, and Russia.
